analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 7 cosponsors, sent to a House committee, and died there without a hearing or a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Secretary from ever issuing a lease to explore for or produce oil, gas, or any mineral in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas — the federal waters off the Atlantic coast from roughly New England through the Carolinas [S2][S3]. That would have permanently closed those waters to offshore drilling, which currently can be opened or closed by whoever sets the nation's leasing plan [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and never moved further before the Congress ended in January 2007 [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Atlantic coastal communities, including beach tourism businesses and commercial and recreational fishing interests, who would be protected from the risk of spills and the industrial activity that accompanies offshore drilling. State and local governments along the coast, and everyone who uses the shore, would benefit from a permanent legal barrier that no future administration could undo by rewriting a leasing plan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coast tourism, fishing, and shore communities

how_it_helps.text: Adds a subsection to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act directing that the Secretary of the Interior 'shall not issue a lease for the exploration, development, or production of oil, natural gas, or any other mineral' in the Mid-Atlantic or North Atlantic planning areas [S3].

Because the ban is written into statute and applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of this section or any other law,' it would take Atlantic drilling off the table permanently rather than leaving it to each administration's five-year leasing choices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would bear the cost of being permanently excluded from Atlantic federal waters, and the nation would forgo whatever oil and gas might have been produced there — a cost felt in energy supply, potential federal leasing revenue, and gasoline and heating-fuel prices at the margin.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that the Atlantic Outer Continental Shelf may hold significant oil and natural gas, and a permanent statutory ban forfeits domestic energy production, federal lease revenue, and some upward pressure on energy prices — a cost borne partly by consumers. Supporters would answer that spill risk to fisheries, beaches, and coastal economies outweighs the recoverable energy, but the trade-off is real.

A statutory ban also removes the possibility of extracting energy with today's much-improved drilling safeguards at some future date; a permanent prohibition cannot be revisited even if technology and conditions change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs to a broad but diffuse public — coastal economies, fisheries, and shoreline users — while its cost falls on a concentrated industry and shows up at the margin in energy supply and prices. The design is simple and enforceable: a flat statutory prohibition on leases in two planning areas. The genuine trade-off is foregone domestic energy and federal revenue versus permanent protection from drilling-related spills and industrialization of the Atlantic coast.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee in April 2005, and nothing further happened before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on April 21, 2005, with 7 cosponsors (6 Democrats, 1 Republican) [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Resources; five days later it was sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee and Interior was asked for its comments [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired with the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Atlantic offshore oil and gas interests came out ahead: with the bill dead, the legal framework for Atlantic leasing stayed open to whatever a future Congress or administration chose to do, and drilling opponents had to keep fighting the same fight each session.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Atlantic offshore oil and gas interests

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.role: Sponsor; U.S. Representative for New Jersey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently bar offshore drilling leases in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas.

for.name: 7 cosponsors (6 House Democrats, 1 House Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the support was enough to move it out of committee.

against.name: House Committee on Resources leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (never scheduled action on the bill)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on April 26, 2005, and took no further action; no hearing or markup occurred during the Congress.

against.name: Energy industry opposition to Atlantic leasing bans
against.role: Opponents of statutory offshore drilling bans
against.what_they_did: Opposed permanent statutory exclusions of Atlantic waters from oil and gas leasing during the 109th Congress, a period when pro-drilling forces were seeking to expand outer continental shelf access.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 6 of 7 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican cosponsor; the bill died in a House committee without a recorded vote, so no roll-call party breakdown exists.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently excluded them from the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas, closing off potential leases and production. Their interest in keeping Atlantic waters available runs against the coastal communities exposed to spill and industrialization risk.

industries.industry: Atlantic coastal tourism and recreation businesses
industries.note: A permanent ban protects the beaches and coastal waters that beach tourism, charter fishing, and shore economies depend on, and that drilling rigs or a spill could damage.
The bill protects fishing grounds and fish habitat in the two planning areas from seismic exploration, drilling activity, and spill risk.
